title: A survey about a new bus route

stimulus.title: A survey about a new bus route
stimulus.html:
A city’s transit agency is planning a new express bus route. The city has four districts, A, B, C and D, and the agency has a complete list of the 48,000 home addresses in the city, organized by district (12,000 in each district). Residents of districts near the planned route may feel very differently about it from residents of districts far from it. The agency considers two ways to gather opinions:

  • Method 1: choose 100 addresses at random from each district’s list and interview one adult at each address.
  • Method 2: post a link on the agency’s website and social media asking residents to vote for or against the new route.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write an investigative question that the agency could answer with data from Method 1.

rubric.point: Names the population (adult residents of the city, or of its households) and the variable (whether they support the new route)
accept: all adult residents of the city

rubric.point: Asks for a parameter that the data can estimate, such as a proportion

parts.sample: What proportion of adult residents of the city support the new express bus route?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify the sampling method used in Method 1, and explain one statistical advantage of it over a simple random sample of 400 addresses from the whole city, in context.

rubric.point: Identifies a stratified random sample, with the districts as strata
Explains that each district is guaranteed representation (100 residents each), which an SRS of 400 may not give
accept: an SRS might by chance include few residents of a district

rubric.point: Connects to context: opinions likely differ by distance from the route, so stratifying by district gives a more precise estimate of the city’s proportion
accept: residents within a district are similar in their opinions, so the estimate varies less
strata are similar inside and differ from each other in support

parts.sample: Method 1 is a stratified random sample with the four districts as strata. Because residents near the route may feel very differently from residents far from it, stratifying by district guarantees that each district is represented by 100 residents, which a simple random sample of 400 from the whole city might not do. Since opinions are likely similar within a district and different between districts, the stratified sample should give a more precise estimate of the proportion of all city residents who support the route.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Identify a source of bias in Method 2, and explain how it would likely affect the estimate of the proportion of residents who support the route.

rubric.point: Identifies voluntary response bias (residents choose whether to respond); undercoverage of residents without internet access is also accepted with a direction

Gives a direction with a reason in context: residents with strong opinions, such as bus riders who want the route or neighbors who oppose construction, are most likely to vote, so the estimate is likely too high (or too low, with a matching reason)
accept: overestimates support because riders who want the route are most motivated to vote
a direction tied to who is likely to respond

parts.sample: Method 2 has voluntary response bias, because residents decide for themselves whether to vote. Residents who ride the bus and want the new route are the most likely to follow the agency online and to bother voting, so the proportion who support the route in the poll would likely be higher than the proportion among all city residents.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe how to use a random number generator to select the 100 addresses from district A’s list of 12,000 addresses, so that someone else could follow your procedure.

rubric.point: Labels the addresses with distinct numbers from 1 to 12,000 and generates random integers from 1 to 12,000
accept: use a random integer generator on 1 to 12,000

rubric.point: Skips repeated numbers and continues until 100 different addresses are chosen, then selects the addresses with those labels

parts.sample: Number the 12,000 addresses in district A from 1 to 12,000. Use a random number generator to produce random integers from 1 to 12,000. Ignore any number that has already been chosen. Continue until 100 different numbers have been chosen, and interview one adult at each of the 100 addresses with those numbers.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Suppose every chosen address in Method 1 responds. To what group can the agency generalize its results? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Generalizes to adult residents of all the city’s addresses (the four districts), because the addresses were chosen at random from a complete list of the city’s addresses
accept: the population of city residents, since random sampling from the full list was used

parts.sample: The agency can generalize to the adult residents at all 48,000 addresses in the city, because the addresses were chosen at random within every district from a complete list of the city’s addresses.
